title: SPE Chapter 07 — PDO
_comment: VET THIS FILE before rendering. lane 'app' = running page (optional 'js' Base API); lane 'code' = self-contained page from local source, lines hl highlighted. App routes assume seeded posts (id 1 exists). Rebuild: RESYNTH=1 bash scripts/make-episode.sh 07-PDO

scenes.narr: Chapter seven gives the application a real database. This list of posts is coming straight out of SQLite.
The schema is plain SQL, and it loads itself the first time the database file is created, seeded with a few rows to start.
The database wrapper extends PDO and sets three defaults that matter: throw on error, fetch associative arrays, and use real prepared statements.
Its constructor opens the SQLite file, turns on foreign keys, and runs that schema only when the file is brand new.
This private method is the one place in the whole app where SQL is prepared and run — every query funnels through here, each value safely bound.
Reads return different shapes depending on what you ask for, chosen by a match expression.
And what you ask for is an enum: all rows, one row, or a single column — no magic strings to mistype.
So finding one post reads almost like English: read from posts, where the id matches, give me one.
Create, update, and delete build their statements from array keys, and each is marked no-discard — so ignoring the result is a mistake the language itself catches.
Writes stay behind the same guard as before: only a valid, token-checked POST reaches the database, and then it redirects.
That is this form — a new post, saved with a prepared insert.
Even the URL slug is built with the pipe operator: lower-case it, strip it to word characters, and add a little randomness for uniqueness.
Read a single post, and it is fetched by id with a bound parameter — never glued into the query as text.
And the whole list is available as JSON, served straight from the database.
That is chapter seven: SQLite through a tiny, safe PDO wrapper. Next, chapter eight adds real users and logins.
